To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

accounting estimates do not improve the quality of financial reporting, as measured by the ability to predict enterprise cash flows, and that estimates improve the quality of earnings reporting, as measured in terms of the ability to predict next year’s earnings.
accounting estimates do not improve the predictability of future cash flows and earnings beyond that provided by accruals from working capital accounts (excluding inventories).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the quality of financial data, as reflected by the ability of financial data to predict future cash flows and earnings, and the role of accounting estimates in improving the usefulness of financial information.
the usefulness of accounting information, particularly accounting estimates, in providing information to investors.
whether accounting estimates improve the relevance of accounting information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the usefulness of estimates in accounting is limited, but not entirely negligible.
estimates in the financial statements are useful to the extent that they are reliable.
the usefulness of financial estimates to investors is mixed and, at times, negative.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
estimates are not useful for predicting future cash flows but are useful for predicting future earnings.
the usefulness of estimates in accounting for the quality of financial statements is not clear.
the usefulness of estimates in predicting cash flows is limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
estimates are not as useful as one would hope.
the use of estimates should be limited to those estimates for which the underlying assumptions are relatively stable over time and for which there are reliable benchmarks.
accounting estimates are a double-edged sword, with the benefits of improved prediction of earnings and cash flows offsetting the costs of reduced comparability and increased information risk.
